# AI Infrastructure Reordering, 2026–2036: A Structural Industry Outlook

### How the AI Compute Buildout Is Reallocating Semiconductors, Memory, Advanced Packaging, Power, Capital, and End-Market Capacity

**Author:** James (kamanager2012)  
**Evidence cutoff:** August 28, 2026  
**Edition revision:** September 14, 2026  
**Analysis and scenario horizon:** 2026–2036  
**Canonical research language:** English  
**Professional Chinese edition:** available

---

## Scope

> **Positioning boundary:** this report does not claim to be globally unique, the world's most comprehensive AI-infrastructure report, or the deepest source on every layer. Specialist research programs in power markets, semiconductor supply chains, compute datasets, sell-side finance, and policy can be materially stronger within their own domains. The report's contribution is the **cross-layer integration** of physical supply, system-stack competition, capital formation, downstream transmission, evidence identity, denominator discipline, and explicit falsification rules.

This report is a 32-chapter long-form industry study of AI infrastructure, semiconductors, memory, advanced packaging, hyperscaler system stacks, power, capital, Agent-Native Software, Physical AI, labor and talent systems, and structural industrial change.

**Analytical hierarchy:** the report is broad by design, but the chapters do not carry equal evidentiary weight. Physical-resource allocation, system substitution, capital formation, and clearing form the load-bearing industrial spine. Agent-native software and Physical AI are demand-side extensions; labor and talent chapters are second-order transmission modules. The full role map is stated in the Table of Contents.

The report separates:

- observed and verifiable facts (F — Fact);
- explicit forward assumptions (H — Hypothesis);
- causal transmission mechanisms (M — Mechanism);
- conditional future states (S — Scenario);
- observable reverse signals that would force judgments to change (X — Falsification).

### Language and editorial architecture

The **English edition is the sole canonical analytical text**. New claims, mechanism definitions, denominator choices, evidence boundaries, scenario language, section order, and falsification logic are resolved in English first because the primary evidence base—filings, earnings materials, product documentation, technical papers, contracts, and industry terminology—is predominantly English.

The Chinese edition is the **professional Chinese translation of the English canonical text**, not an independent analytical edition. Chinese syntax may be localized and standard industry terms such as HBM, CoWoS, CapEx, TCO, utilization, qualification, system stack, scale-up / scale-out, and workload may remain in English when that preserves precision. The translation must not independently add, remove, reorder, or redefine claims, mechanisms, denominators, evidence identities, scenarios, falsification boundaries, or section hierarchy. Any substantive revision is made in English first and then translated into Chinese.

Editorial rule:

> **Simplify navigation, not analysis. Do not explain what the target professional reader is expected to know; explain what is easy to mis-measure, mis-denominate, or infer incorrectly.**

The objective is not to produce a single deterministic 2036 forecast. It is to build an industrial-analysis framework whose judgments can be tested against later public evidence. Facts emerging after **August 28, 2026** belong to a later evidence cycle; they may be used to re-evaluate the framework, but they are not backdated into this edition's evidence set.

**Title lineage.** The repository slug and historical shorthand name `ai-infra-hegemony` refer to the research question, not to a current finding. The report's evidence-based baseline is S2 — Baseline Concentration; S3 — Resource Hegemony is a conditional hypothesis. The site title `AI Infrastructure Reordering` is the canonical name.


### Entry point for end-system and industrial-supply readers

This report is not arguing that “only AI matters.” Smartphones, PCs, game consoles, vehicles, industrial equipment, robotics, and long-lifecycle high-reliability electronics remain important.

The core question is:

> **When AI/HPC demand with higher willingness to pay, longer capacity commitments, and stronger capital formation changes the priority of shared or adjacent upstream resources, can non-AI end systems still obtain enough, stable, affordable supply on their own BOM, qualification, lifecycle, and product cadence?**

If you come from consumer electronics, game consoles, automotive, industrial systems, robotics, or high-reliability supply chains, a useful first pass is:

**Ch01 → Ch03 → Ch21 → Ch20 §10 → Ch32**

NVIDIA's system stack, hyperscalers, China's parallel stack, and S1–S4 can be read on a second pass as mechanism background.

## Evidence boundary

The report relies primarily on:

- annual reports, 10-K / 20-F filings, quarterly results, and official investor materials;
- regulatory, court, and government documents;
- formal contracts and project disclosures;
- official product specifications and technical documentation;
- high-quality institutional research;
- report-side models and stress tests when explicitly labeled.

Institutional forecasts, sell-side estimates, and report-side calculations are not promoted into company facts.

## Disclaimer

This report is for industry research and information purposes only. It is not investment advice, a securities rating, legal advice, an audit opinion, or a recommendation to enter into any transaction. All forward-looking judgments are conditional and may change with technology, demand, capital, regulation, geopolitics, and supply.

## Copyright and License

Original report text is distributed under the **[MIT License](../../LICENSE)** (see [Chinese Guide & Commercial Reuse Notice](../../LICENSE.zh-CN.md)), permitting free reproduction, commercial use, and adaptation subject to retaining original copyright attribution (`Copyright (c) 2026 James Oldman`). Third-party material remains subject to the rights and licensing terms of its respective owners. Third-party material is used only when its rights boundary is clear and the material is appropriately cited or otherwise permitted.

Ch25–Ch26 (labor and education) are **second-order transmission / extended-impact chapters**. They examine how infrastructure change can propagate into labor and talent systems, but they are not load-bearing inputs to the S1–S4 scenario framework.

The 32 chapters do **not** carry equal evidentiary weight. Their roles are:

- **Synthesis:** Ch01, Ch32 — compress the judgment; they do not create independent evidence by repetition.

- **Method and evaluation:** Ch27–Ch31 — define evidence rules, monitoring, scenarios, milestones, and strategic optionality rather than adding another physical bottleneck.

1. [Figure 1 — The competitive unit is the system stack](figures/fig-01-system-stack.svg)  
   **Type:** report framework. **Primary analytical homes:** Ch02, Ch12, Ch32.

2. [Figure 2 — Non-AI Residual Capacity (NARC)](figures/fig-02-narc-mechanism.svg)  
   **Type:** report-side analytical definition. **Primary analytical homes:** Ch03, Ch08, Ch21, Ch32.

3. [Figure 3 — HBM3E wafer-supply intensity versus DDR5](figures/fig-03-hbm-wafer-intensity.svg)  
   **Type:** first-party physical trade ratio. **Source:** Micron FY24 Q2 Prepared Remarks.  
   **Boundary:** same technology node / same number of bits; ≈3× wafer supply is not a price multiple and not a permanent constant for every HBM generation.

4. [Figure 4 — NVIDIA forward supply / capacity commitment family in 2026](figures/fig-04-nvidia-forward-commitments.svg)  
   **Type:** first-party filing data. **Values:** US$95.2B (Jan 25), US$119B (Apr 26), US$279B (Jul 26).  
   **Boundary:** reporting labels, mix, and duration are not identical across dates; no supplier-level split; commitment is not realized supplier revenue or delivered capacity.

5. [Figure 5 — Power / LPS delivery-state model](figures/fig-05-power-state-machine.svg)  
   **Type:** report framework. **Primary analytical homes:** Ch07, Ch08, Ch29, Ch32.  
   **Boundary:** secured / contracted ≠ energized ≠ utilized; IT-GW ≠ generation GW ≠ PPA capacity.

6. [Figure 6 — S1–S4 scenario map](figures/fig-06-s1-s4-scenario-map.svg)  
   **Type:** report scenario framework. **Primary analytical home:** Ch30.  
   **Boundary:** scenarios are parallel conditional states with no fixed probabilities; S2 is highlighted only as the August 2026 evidence baseline.

7. [Figure 7 — TSMC 2Q26 demand and technology mix](figures/fig-07-tsmc-2q26-mix.svg)  
   **Type:** first-party actual data with separate denominators. **Primary analytical home:** Ch04.  
   **Boundary:** HPC 66% and smartphone 22% are shares of total revenue; 7 nm and below 77% is a share of wafer revenue. None is customer-level wafer allocation.

8. [Figure 8 — Rolling Bottleneck Cascade](figures/fig-08-rolling-bottleneck-cascade.svg)  
   **Type:** report framework. **Primary analytical homes:** Ch06–Ch08, Ch19, Ch24, Ch30.  
   **Boundary:** causal schematic, not a deterministic sequence or timing forecast; the binding bottleneck can migrate and need not remain in the same layer.

9. [Figure 9 — Anchor demand and Financing Reflexivity](figures/fig-09-financing-reflexivity.svg)  
   **Type:** report financing framework. **Primary analytical homes:** Ch13, Ch23, Ch24.  
   **Evidence anchors:** NVIDIA PORTS-Pike maximum conditional guarantee exposure US$105B; AMD maximum gross commercial-partner lease-guarantee exposure US$4.1B.  
   **Boundary:** both are maximum guarantee exposures—not funded CapEx or additive demand totals; interpretation depends on utilization, monetization, independent risk capital, and refinancing conditions.

10. [Figure 10 — Demand-side closure through verified workflow output](figures/fig-10-verified-workflow-loop.svg)  
    **Type:** report economic framework. **Primary analytical homes:** Ch14, Ch19, Ch24, Ch32.  
    **Boundary:** verified workflow output is a long-run economic criterion, not an empirically calibrated fact metric as of the evidence cutoff.

11. [Figure 11 — Production-Grade Parallel Stack vs. Autonomous Frontier Closure](figures/fig-11-china-closure-gates.svg)  
    **Type:** report closure-test framework. **Primary analytical homes:** Ch17, Ch32.  
    **Current evidence:** partial production deployment is real, but public evidence does not close all seven Production-Grade Gates.  
    **Boundary:** production-grade substitution ≠ full technological autonomy; import dependence also does not prove absence of a production-grade parallel stack.

## Publication note

These figures are part of the publication layer. They do not reopen the frozen 32-chapter research logic. Any future quantitative figure that requires a new denominator, new estimate, or new factual claim must be treated as new research rather than as editorial illustration.

# Abbreviations and Core Glossary

## Industry abbreviations

| Abbreviation / term | Meaning | Usage boundary in this report |
|---|---|---|
| AI | Artificial Intelligence | Generative / frontier AI only when context makes that scope explicit |
| HPC | High-Performance Computing | Includes AI/HPC workloads; not synonymous with AI |
| GPU | Graphics Processing Unit | Data-center and consumer layers remain distinct |
| CPU | Central Processing Unit | Not interchangeable with accelerators |
| ASIC | Application-Specific Integrated Circuit | Cloud custom accelerators are one important form |
| SoC | System on Chip | Common in smartphone, edge, and embedded systems |
| IC | Integrated Circuit | Generic component layer; process node, packaging, and system integration remain separate variables |
| HBM | High Bandwidth Memory | Bit share, wafer input, and market share remain separate denominators |
| DRAM | Dynamic Random-Access Memory | HBM, DDR, LPDDR, and RDIMM remain product-level distinctions |
| DDR5 | Double Data Rate 5 SDRAM | One conventional-DRAM product class |
| RDIMM | Registered DIMM | Server memory; not equivalent to HBM |
| LPDDR | Low-Power DDR | Used mainly in mobile/client systems and selected rack CPU memory |
| GDDR | Graphics Double Data Rate memory | Common in gaming GPUs / game consoles; not treated as the same product pool as HBM |
| NAND | NAND Flash | Different memory technology from DRAM/HBM |
| eSSD | Enterprise SSD | Enterprise solid-state storage |
| NVMe | Non-Volatile Memory Express | High-speed SSD interface / protocol; a product specification is not an industry-supply measure |
| UFS | Universal Flash Storage | Mobile / embedded / selected game-console storage; analyzed separately from data-center SSD |
| HDD | Hard Disk Drive | Conventional storage; a different supply pool from NAND / eSSD |
| CoWoS | Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate | TSMC advanced-packaging family; customer allocation is not inferred from revenue share |
| TSV | Through-Silicon Via | Important in HBM stacking / 3D integration |
| HVM | High-Volume Manufacturing | Qualification-to-volume transition; qualification status is not HVM |
| CUDA | NVIDIA compute platform / programming ecosystem | Analyzed as a software switching-cost variable |
| NVLink / NVSwitch | NVIDIA scale-up interconnect technologies | Not treated as the same layer as scale-out networking |
| API | Application Programming Interface | Software integration surface; one variable-cost component of agent-native workflows |
| CapEx | Capital Expenditure | Guidance, expectation, and actuals remain separate |
| OpEx | Operating Expenditure | Not mechanically combined with CapEx |
| FCF | Free Cash Flow | Company-defined and GAAP/non-GAAP identities are preserved |
| PPA | Power Purchase Agreement | Contracted capacity is not energized/utilized load |
| PUE | Power Usage Effectiveness | Data-center efficiency metric |
| LPS | Land, Power and Shell | Site land, power access, and building shell; secured LPS is not energized / utilized compute |
| IT-GW | Gigawatts of IT load / IT capacity | Design capacity for IT equipment / AI factory load; not interchangeable with generation GW, PPA GW, or grid-delivered GW |
| CSP | Cloud Service Provider | Hyperscalers are an important subset |
| OEM | Original Equipment Manufacturer | End-device / system manufacturer |
| ODM | Original Design Manufacturer | Design-and-manufacturing service provider |
| PC | Personal Computer | Traditional client end system; one NARC-relevant demand pool |
| BOM | Bill of Materials | Used in end-market cost-transmission analysis |
| TCO | Total Cost of Ownership | Preferred system-level comparison unit |
| ASP | Average Selling Price | Product and time denominator must be explicit |
| SKU | Stock-Keeping Unit | Product-configuration unit; SKU count is not a volume or supply measure |
| ROI | Return on Investment | Report-side usage only; not a disclosed company metric unless a source is named |
| GAAP | U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles | GAAP and non-GAAP identities are never merged |
| PPE | Property, Plant and Equipment | Used in hyperscaler capital-base reconstruction; accounting line items differ by company |
| TTM | Trailing Twelve Months | The time window must be stated; not directly comparable with calendar guidance |
| TAM | Total Addressable Market | Institutional / sell-side estimates only; not a disclosed actual |
| EOL | End of Life | Product-continuity risk in long-lifecycle end systems |
| MCU | Microcontroller Unit | Automotive / industrial layer; not a frontier-AI accelerator |
| APU | Accelerated Processing Unit | Console / client SoC context; not an HBM-class AI system |
| RF | Radio Frequency | Aerospace / defense special-process exposure |
| ADAS | Advanced Driver Assistance Systems | Automotive compute context |
| FLOPS | Floating-Point Operations per Second | Peak compute only; not a workload denominator (see [Chapter 8](part-I-ch08-quantitative-framework.md)) |
| KV cache | Key-Value cache | Inference memory state; one reason inference can remain memory-bound |
| EUV / DUV | Extreme / Deep Ultraviolet lithography | Process-equipment layer; relevant to export controls |

## Standard units

- Data capacity: KB / MB / GB / TB / PB / EB
- Bits and transfer rates: Kb / Mb / Gb / Tb; Mb/s / Gb/s / Tb/s
- Power: W / kW / MW / GW
- Energy: Wh / kWh / MWh / TWh
- Frequency: Hz / kHz / MHz / GHz
- Process / dimensions: nm / μm / mm / mm²
- U.S. dollar values: preserve source precision where material, e.g. US$96.221B and US$279B

## Core analytical concepts

### Resource reallocation pressure
Shorthand for the mechanism by which higher willingness to pay, longer-duration orders, and stronger expected returns from AI/HPC can redirect scarce capital and physical resources toward AI/HPC uses. It is descriptive mechanism language, not a separate empirical law.

### Scarce-layer Value Capture
Value capture arising in layers with low supply elasticity and difficult substitution, strengthened by scarcity, switching costs, and supply coordination. It is not a legal monopoly finding.

### Non-AI Residual Capacity (NARC)
Effective supply available to non-AI markets after AI / Anchor Buyer demand and other priority demand have been allocated.

### Quantity Assurance
Whether a buyer can obtain enough qualified supply on schedule within the relevant quality, generation, qualification, and delivery window. It is distinct from Price Pressure: **willingness to pay more does not guarantee planned quantity.**

### Upgrade Tax
An analytical term, not a tax category. It describes an end-system outcome in which higher upstream opportunity cost produces **slower specification improvement at the same price band, or a higher BOM / weaker subsidy for the same target specification**. It must not be generalized into uniform price inflation across all end markets.

### Two-speed semiconductor economics
Descriptive shorthand for the divergence created when the AI Infrastructure Economy and Traditional Device Economy share parts of the same upstream resource base but differ in willingness to pay, contract duration, BOM constraints, and capital-formation power.

### AI Capacity Gap / AI Capacity Growth Gap
**AI Capacity Gap** is the absolute physical shortfall `AI effective demand − AI effective capacity` within the same layer and delivery window; **AI Capacity Growth Gap** is the difference between demand growth and effective-capacity growth and describes only the direction in which the gap is changing. The two are not interchangeable.

### Incremental Scarce-Capacity Access
A layer-specific framework for evaluating whether different buyers can repeatedly obtain sufficient, qualified, and timely supply in advanced logic, HBM/DRAM, advanced packaging, networking, LPS, and energized power.

It is measured through variables such as qualified suppliers, lead time, allocation fulfillment, long-term agreements/prepayments, delivery schedules, buyer credit quality, and supply elasticity. The report does not compress different physical pools into one synthetic cross-layer percentage.

### Cloud system-stack substitution
An economic substitution test for whether hyperscalers can combine custom accelerators, interconnect, compiler/runtime, racks/pods, and captive workloads into a production-grade alternative system stack.

### Anchor-buyer mechanism
The mechanism by which long-duration compute commitments from large model companies influence data-center, power, chip, memory, and project-financing buildout. It is a demand-formation mechanism, not a separate grand theory.

### Rolling Bottleneck Cascade
The dynamic rotation of the binding constraint across logic, HBM, advanced packaging, networking, power, utilization, and related layers.

### AI inheritance
Shorthand for the mechanism by which AI adds an intelligence / automation layer on top of an existing digital installed base of software, databases, cloud systems, APIs, digital documents, source code, identity/access systems, and workflows. Highly digitized organizations can therefore face lower marginal Digital → AI deployment friction, but **not zero friction**: data quality, integration, security, governance, responsibility, reliability, human review, and unit economics still determine production adoption.

### AI Software Unit Economics
A workflow-level cost framework incorporating inference, retrieval/storage, tools/APIs, retries, human review, and other variable AI costs.

### Financing Reflexivity
The feedback mechanism created when a system seller also uses equity investment, credit enhancement, LPS support, or compute-financing coordination to accelerate customer and infrastructure buildout. It does not prove demand is artificial; it changes how demand independence, risk transfer, and refinancing dependence should be evaluated.

### Production-Grade Parallel Stack
A substitute system that can sustain real production workloads across accelerator / compute, memory subsystem, advanced packaging, interconnect, compiler/runtime, production workload, and utilization / reliability / economics. It does not require every upstream input to be fully autonomous.

### Autonomous Frontier Closure
A higher closure standard in which the system can continue scaling and iterating across generations when critical external inputs are constrained. In addition to a production-grade stack, it requires advanced-manufacturing continuity, equipment / materials / software / service continuity, and durable HBM, packaging, power, LPS, and capital formation.

### Time-to-Power
The time required for a site or project to obtain physically deliverable power. It must remain separate from headline generation capacity, PPA capacity, secured LPS, and future IT-GW design capacity.

### Verified Workflow Output
An AI-assisted workflow outcome that has passed the quality, responsibility, or business-acceptance conditions required for repeatable delivery, billing, or production use. It is the report's demand-side unit linking compute cost, enterprise adoption, cash flow, and capital recovery.

### Task-to-Job Translation
Model Capability → Task Suitability → Workflow Redesign → Adoption Economics / Responsibility → Job Composition → Employment / Wage Outcome. Prevents technical exposure rates from being converted directly into job-loss rates.

## Scenario terminology

- **S1 — Competitive Expansion:** higher supply elasticity, multi-sourcing, and portability distribute value capture more broadly.
- **S2 — Baseline Concentration:** a small number of system platforms / scarce-layer suppliers retain strong economics while real substitution paths continue developing.
- **S3 — Resource Hegemony:** multi-layer scarcity, concentrated quantity assurance / delivery access, switching costs, and financing coordination strengthen together while workload monetization remains sufficient to support associated long-duration commitments, materially raising the cost of replicating the full infrastructure stack.
- **S4 — Capital Hard Landing:** accounting losses, utilization/revenue, market clearing, forward commitments, and demand-financing quality deteriorate broadly and persistently, producing capital clearing.

## Evidence identity

- **F — Fact:** already occurred and publicly verifiable.
- **H — Hypothesis:** explicit forward assumption.
- **M — Mechanism:** causal transmission path.
- **S — Scenario:** conditional future state.
- **X — Falsification:** reverse signal strong enough to force a judgment change.
- **A:** first-party / formal evidence.
- **B:** institutional research.
- **C:** sell-side / supply-chain / media estimate.
- **D:** report model / arithmetic / sensitivity / stress test.

# Competitive Set, Substitution Paths, and Counter-Evidence Matrix

> This matrix prevents the “hegemony” thesis from being supported only by evidence about one platform's strengths. It does not treat every company as a direct competitor in one market; competition is defined separately by physical layer, system layer, and end market.

| Analytical layer | Primary observed set | Main substitutes / competitors | Core comparison metrics | Required counter-evidence / boundary | Main chapters |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| General-purpose AI system stack | NVIDIA | Google TPU/Ironwood, AWS Trainium, Microsoft Maia, Meta MTIA, AMD Instinct/ROCm | production workload, external availability, migration cost, system utilization, TCO, supply assurance | custom silicon is already a real second route; one-chip benchmarks do not prove full system substitution | [Ch02](part-I-ch02-nvidia-system-stack.md), [Ch12](part-II-ch12-hyperscaler-system-stack.md), [Ch16](part-II-ch16-differentiated-competitors.md) |
| Advanced logic | TSMC | Samsung Foundry, Intel Foundry, SMIC, and future qualified second sources | qualified node, volume, yield disclosure, customer diversity, time-to-capacity | foundry revenue share ≠ frontier yield/node capacity; HPC share ≠ AI share | [Ch04](part-I-ch04-tsmc-advanced-logic.md), [Ch09](part-I-ch09-semiconductor-redundancy.md), [Ch17](part-II-ch17-china-parallel-stack.md) |
| HBM / DRAM | SK hynix, Samsung, Micron | conventional-DRAM economics, CXMT conventional DRAM, future HBM entrants | HBM qualification, bits/wafer input, product mix, contract pricing, allocation fulfillment | DDR/RDIMM per-wafer economics can recover; HBM resource pull is not infinitely one-directional | [Ch05](part-I-ch05-hbm-memory.md), [Ch21](part-III-ch21-consumer-transmission.md) |
| Advanced packaging | TSMC CoWoS | Samsung/Intel packaging, OSAT expansion, alternative integration architectures | qualified capacity, lead time, yield/throughput disclosure, customer access | customer-level CoWoS allocation is undisclosed; B-grade demand share cannot become TSMC fact | [Ch06](part-I-ch06-advanced-packaging.md) |
| Interconnect / software | CUDA/NVLink/NVSwitch ecosystem | ROCm, XLA/TPU stack, AWS Neuron, open compiler/runtime, alternative fabrics | migration cost, framework coverage, cluster scale, debuggability, production uptime | proprietary stacks can be bypassed for selected workloads; “runs” does not mean low migration cost | [Ch02](part-I-ch02-nvidia-system-stack.md), [Ch12](part-II-ch12-hyperscaler-system-stack.md), [Ch16](part-II-ch16-differentiated-competitors.md) |
| Developer distribution / open-model hub | Hugging Face reported transaction / NVIDIA | alternative model hubs, self-hosted registries, Git/GitHub distribution, framework-native registries, cloud marketplaces | default ranking, multi-vendor parity, runtime/backend neutrality, artifact portability, mirrorability, deployment friction | Aug-27-2026 evidence is only a Reuters report citing The Information; no formal closing/approval evidence in the cutoff set; open-weight assets can mirror/multi-home; hub control ≠ automatic ownership of model IP or all developer traffic | [Ch02](part-I-ch02-nvidia-system-stack.md), [Ch18](part-II-ch18-antitrust-policy.md) |
| Power / LPS / powered land | hyperscaler / AI-campus demand | utility expansion, restart projects, SMR / nuclear, grid/transmission buildout, LPS development | Announced→Contracted/Secured→Permitted→Construction→Energized→Utilized, Time-to-Power | generation GW, PPA GW, and IT-GW are not mechanically interchangeable; headline capacity cannot be summed into active AI load | [Ch07](part-I-ch07-power-constraint.md) |
| Model-company demand | OpenAI, Anthropic, other Anchor Buyers | hyperscaler internal workloads, enterprise demand, sovereign demand | contract duration, delivered capacity, utilization, monetization, financing support | long-duration commitments improve buildout certainty and can also amplify duration mismatch | [Ch13](part-II-ch13-anchor-compute-buyer.md), [Ch23](part-III-ch23-capital-financing.md) |
| China parallel / frontier stack | domestic accelerator/software/memory/foundry ecosystem | global frontier stack plus domestic consumer/general-compute substitutes | production-grade: accelerator, memory subsystem, packaging, interconnect, compiler/runtime, production workload, system economics; autonomous closure separately tests equipment/material/service continuity and multi-generation infrastructure capital | conventional DRAM/NAND or smartphone substitution does not prove autonomous frontier closure; external dependencies do not erase observable partial production deployment / substitution, but a complete production-grade frontier closure still requires gate-by-gate validation | [Ch17](part-II-ch17-china-parallel-stack.md) |
| Client / edge AI | Apple, Qualcomm, AMD, Intel | local inference, hybrid cloud-edge, NVIDIA edge products | performance/W, memory footprint, OS integration, distribution, privacy/latency | data-center system economics cannot be copied directly into battery/power-constrained edge markets | [Ch15](part-II-ch15-physical-ai.md), [Ch16](part-II-ch16-differentiated-competitors.md) |
| Capital cycle | hyperscalers, system sellers, memory/foundry/power projects | capacity overshoot / ROI shock as counter-scenarios | utilization, D&A, FCF, clearing price, commitments, asset duration, supplier-assisted financing | high CapEx can be a moat or a future write-down source; independently financed end demand must be separated from supplier equity / credit support | [Ch19](part-III-ch19-capex-supercycle.md), [Ch22](part-III-ch22-depreciation-wall.md), [Ch23](part-III-ch23-capital-financing.md), [Ch24](part-III-ch24-capital-clearing.md) |

## Use rules

1. Any dominance/hegemony judgment must answer at least four questions: **does substitution exist, what is migration cost, can scarce inputs be multi-sourced, and is price feedback working?**
2. Competitive sets are layer-specific; smartphone SoCs, frontier-training accelerators, foundries, and HBM vendors must not be forced into one market-share table.
3. “No equivalent substitute” and “no substitute at all” are different statements.
4. Every major update should inspect at least one piece of evidence that could **weaken** the main thesis rather than only adding supportive evidence.
5. If counter-evidence becomes persistent, comparable, sufficiently independent, and changes a core mechanism variable, S1–S4 weighting must change rather than burying the evidence in a footnote.

# Research Brief

## AI Infrastructure Reordering, 2026–2036

**Structural industry outlook on system-stack competition, semiconductor allocation, HBM, advanced packaging, power, capital formation, and end-market transmission**

**Evidence cutoff:** August 28, 2026  
**Edition revision:** September 14, 2026  
**Status:** publication-layer brief derived from the frozen 32-chapter canonical English report. It does not introduce a second analytical edition or new factual claims.

---

## Executive thesis

The AI infrastructure cycle is no longer best understood as a contest over the fastest accelerator.

The relevant competitive unit has shifted toward the complete production system:

> **advanced logic + HBM + advanced packaging + interconnect + compiler/runtime + rack/data center + power/LPS + capital + production workload**

That shift changes the industrial question. The central issue is not whether aggregate semiconductor or infrastructure supply grows. It is **which demand pools obtain the next unit of qualified capacity, how quickly bottlenecks move across layers, and whether installed compute ultimately converts into utilization, workflow output, revenue, and capital recovery.**

As of the report cutoff, the evidence mix is closest to **S2 — Baseline Concentration**:

> **high growth, strong leading platforms, scarce-layer concentration, and credible but incomplete substitution paths coexist.**

This is not a deterministic 2036 forecast. It is the current state that best fits the observed evidence under the report's scenario framework. The repository name and the historical "hegemony" label appear in the title lineage as the research question, not as a current finding; S3 — Resource Hegemony remains a conditional hypothesis with explicit reverse signals.

![Figure 1 — The competitive unit is the system stack](figures/fig-01-system-stack.svg)

---

## 1. What is structurally different in 2026

Three changes matter most.

### 1.1 Platform competition has expanded into system competition

NVIDIA's current advantage is not adequately described by standalone GPU performance. Rack-scale systems combine accelerator compute, HBM, scale-up fabric, software, rack architecture, cooling, deployment tooling, and production migration cost.

Hyperscaler alternatives matter for the same reason. Google, AWS, Microsoft, Meta, and other system builders are not merely introducing alternative chips; they are trying to close enough of the surrounding stack that meaningful production workloads can move.

The relevant competitive test is therefore:

> **Can an alternative stack deliver production workloads with acceptable migration cost, utilization, reliability, supply assurance, and total economics?**

Neither a cheaper die nor a stronger isolated benchmark is sufficient by itself.

### 1.2 AI/HPC is changing the marginal destination of capital

TSMC reported that HPC represented **66% of 2Q26 revenue**, while 7 nm and below represented **77% of wafer revenue**.[^rb1] These measures do not prove customer-level wafer allocation, but they show the economic weight of advanced-compute demand in the foundry mix.

The report describes the resulting structure as a **Two-Speed Semiconductor Economy**:

- AI infrastructure demand can carry high willingness to pay, long commitments, prepayment capacity, and strong capital formation;
- traditional end systems remain important but may operate with lower bidding power, longer qualification clocks, and tighter BOM constraints.

The key variable is therefore not current capacity alone, but **which demand pool is increasingly able to induce the next increment of capacity.**

### 1.3 Gross supply and residual access are different variables

A market can add wafer, DRAM, packaging, or power capacity while traditional buyers still face weaker allocation, higher prices, or slower configuration upgrades.

The report therefore uses **Non-AI Residual Capacity (NARC)**:

```text
NonAI_Residual
= Effective_Supply
- AI_Server_Absorption
- Other_Priority_Demand
```

![Figure 2 — Non-AI Residual Capacity](figures/fig-02-narc-mechanism.svg)

NARC is not a single universal percentage. It must be evaluated separately for each physical pool and qualification boundary.

---

## 2. The physical bottleneck is a moving system, not one permanent scarce component

The report rejects the idea that one layer—GPU, HBM, CoWoS, or power—must remain the dominant bottleneck for the entire decade.

Instead, the system can experience a **Rolling Bottleneck Cascade**:

> memory / packaging tightness → hardware delivery constraint → supply expansion → more systems reach sites → power / interconnection becomes binding → deployment slows → utilization and next-cycle commitments respond

The bottleneck can also move in the opposite direction if capacity is overbuilt relative to demand.

This matters because capital, procurement, and industrial strategy can be wrong even when the diagnosis of one layer is correct. A company can solve yesterday's bottleneck and still fail to deliver a usable system.

### HBM illustrates why denominator discipline matters

Micron disclosed that under a **same technology node / same number of bits** comparison, HBM3E requires approximately **3× the wafer supply of DDR5**.[^rb2]

![Figure 3 — HBM3E wafer-supply intensity versus DDR5](figures/fig-03-hbm-wafer-intensity.svg)

This is a physical manufacturing trade ratio.

It is **not**:

- a price multiple;
- a claim that every HBM generation will require exactly 3×;
- a license to infer HBM economics from bit share alone.

The report keeps HBM bits, DRAM wafer input, packaging capacity, and rack deployment as separate denominators unless public evidence closes them on the same scope.

---

## 3. Forward commitments have become an industrial signal

When direct customer-level HBM, packaging, or rack allocation is unavailable, forward commitments provide a more defensible indicator of resource-reservation intensity than assumption-driven fleet arithmetic.

NVIDIA's disclosed **forward supply / capacity commitment family** rose across reporting dates from:[^rb3]

- **US$95.2B** on January 25, 2026;
- **US$119B** on April 26, 2026;
- **US$279B** on July 26, 2026.

The reporting label, mix, and duration are not identical across dates: the FY26 Form 10-K uses **manufacturing, supply, and capacity commitments**, while the FY27 Q2 Form 10-Q reports **supply and capacity commitments**. The sequence is therefore a forward-reservation indicator, not a homogeneous accounting time series.

![Figure 4 — NVIDIA forward commitments in 2026](figures/fig-04-nvidia-forward-commitments.svg)

The July figure is an aggregate company commitment. Public filings do not provide a supplier-level split.

The analytical implication is narrower but important:

> **high system economics can translate into stronger forward reservation power, which can improve delivery certainty across future system generations.**

This mechanism is self-reinforcing only while utilization, customer demand, financing quality, and supplier economics remain supportive.

---

## 4. Power has become part of compute delivery

Power should not be analyzed merely as an electricity-price input.

At modern rack densities, the limiting variable becomes **Time-to-Power**: how long it takes to move from project intent to energized, usable capacity for a real workload.

The report separates six project states:

![Figure 5 — Power and LPS delivery-state model](figures/fig-05-power-state-machine.svg)

The boundary is critical:

> **secured / contracted capacity ≠ energized capacity ≠ utilized AI load**

and:

> **IT-GW ≠ generation GW ≠ PPA capacity**

The PORTS-Pike structure is analytically important because it shows land, power, shell, credit support, and model-company demand being coordinated earlier in the infrastructure cycle. But its initial **4.25 IT-GW design capacity** remains planned future capacity, not current utilized AI load.[^rb4]

The industrial advantage is therefore not simply “having power.” It is being able to move qualified projects through permitting, interconnection, equipment procurement, construction, energization, and utilization inside the relevant hardware-generation window.

---

## 5. Model companies and capital markets are moving upstream

Leading model companies increasingly influence infrastructure formation rather than consuming only pre-existing cloud capacity.

The report calls this the **Anchor Compute Buyer Effect**:

> **long-duration workload demand → revenue visibility → financing certainty → earlier infrastructure buildout → earlier resource reservation**

This can strengthen the buildout when demand is durable and utilization follows.

It can also increase concentration, duration mismatch, and financing correlation.

The 2026 infrastructure-finance layer adds a second mechanism: **Financing Reflexivity**. Seller equity, credit enhancement, infrastructure support, and third-party capital can accelerate deployment, but they also make demand quality more dependent on financing structure.

PORTS-Pike makes the scale and boundary concrete: NVIDIA's FY27 Q2 Form 10-Q caps aggregate guarantee obligations at **US$105B** for leases covering approximately **4.25 GW of IT load**, with phased activation as data centers enter service. This is maximum conditional credit exposure, **not funded CapEx or current cash outflow**.[^rb5]

AMD provides an independent cross-vendor check: its Q2 2026 Form 10-Q reports **US$4.1B of maximum gross exposure** from guarantees tied to certain commercial-partner data-center lease obligations with terms up to 15 years. This is also maximum guarantee exposure rather than funded CapEx or realized loss.[^rb7] The financing mechanism is therefore broader than one supplier, while the instruments' denominators remain non-additive.

The report therefore distinguishes among:

1. independently financed end demand;
2. long-duration Anchor Buyer commitments;
3. third-party infrastructure capital;
4. supplier equity / credit support.

Large CapEx alone does not by itself establish either durable demand or a bubble.

The relevant question is whether the capital base is validated by **utilization, revenue, market clearing, customer cash generation, financing quality, and verified workflow output.**

---

## 6. Infrastructure demand must close through verified workflow output

A report that stops at GPUs, HBM, CapEx, or data-center capacity is incomplete. Those are the supply side. The ten-year industrial cycle ultimately depends on whether installed compute moves through software, enterprise workflows, and the physical world into verifiable economic output.

The relevant unit is:

> **cost per verified workflow outcome**

**AI inheritance.** Decades of information technology have already created software, databases, cloud systems, APIs, source code, identity/access systems, and traceable workflows. In highly digitized organizations AI can act as an intelligence / automation layer on that installed base:

> **Digital Installed Base → AI Overlay → Workflow Penetration → Automation Depth → Workload Volume**

**Agent-native software.** Traditional SaaS scales largely around accounts and seats; agent-native software continuously consumes inference, retrieval, tools/APIs, retries, observability, and human review. Cheaper models and better routing can cut resource intensity per attempt, but if lower prices unlock more users, longer agent loops, more tool calls, and previously uneconomic workflows, total compute demand can still expand.

**Physical AI** must clear a capital-payback test: the commercial threshold is not one completed task, but whether **Useful Tasks × Uptime × Deployment Scale** can cover **Energy + Maintenance + Human Supervision + Depreciation + Financing**.

**Labor.** Occupational exposure cannot be converted directly into job-loss forecasts; the chain runs through task suitability, workflow redesign, adoption economics, and responsibility.

Lower unit compute cost therefore does not by itself establish either lower total infrastructure demand or a Jevons-style increase in demand. Both depend on whether cheaper compute unlocks more verified workflows. If the supply, capital, and financing layers expand persistently faster than verified output, cash flow, and utilization, the risk of **S4 — Capital Hard Landing** rises structurally.

The demand-side loop is:

> **Physical Infrastructure → System Delivery → Workflow Economics → Verified Output → Adoption / Cash Flow → Utilization → Capital Reinvestment**

![Figure 10 — Demand-side closure through verified workflow output](figures/fig-10-verified-workflow-loop.svg)

---

## 7. Traditional end systems remain important but may lose upstream priority

The report does not argue that smartphones, PCs, game consoles, vehicles, industrial equipment, robotics, aerospace, or other long-lifecycle systems become irrelevant.

The industrial risk lies elsewhere:

> **importance to end users does not automatically guarantee priority in upstream capital allocation.**

Exposure also differs by end market.

- Smartphones, PCs, and selected edge / ADAS systems can share advanced logic, memory, or selected packaging more directly with AI.
- Automotive and industrial systems are often affected through product mix, qualification rigidity, long lifecycle, and supplier allocation.
- Aerospace, defense, and other high-reliability low-volume systems can face continuity risk through mature-node economics, trusted supply, equipment, engineering talent, and special-process availability rather than direct HBM competition.

The relevant transmission channels are therefore:

- quantity assurance;
- lead time;
- configuration / memory-content decisions;
- component pricing;
- qualification flexibility;
- supplier product-mix incentives;
- lifecycle support.

This is why the report tracks **residual qualified supply**, not only global capacity growth.

---

## 8. China requires two separate closure tests

The report separates two questions that are often collapsed.

### Production-Grade Parallel Stack

Can an alternative system run real production workloads across:

- accelerator / compute;
- HBM-class or equivalent memory subsystem;
- advanced packaging;
- high-speed interconnect;
- compiler/runtime;
- production workload;
- utilization, reliability, and economics?

### Autonomous Frontier Closure

Can that stack continue scaling across generations when critical external inputs are constrained?

This additionally requires durable continuity across:

- advanced manufacturing;
- equipment, materials, software, and service;
- HBM / packaging;
- cross-generation process upgrades;
- power / LPS;
- capital formation.

A real production-grade parallel stack can exist without proving autonomous frontier closure.

At the August 28, 2026 evidence cutoff, China has a real frontier parallel stack with partial production deployment, but public evidence remains insufficient to confirm closure across all seven Production-Grade Gates. Autonomous Frontier Closure remains a still higher and unproven threshold.

Conversely, import dependence does not mean no production substitution exists.

---

## 9. The 2026–2036 outlook is conditional

The report uses four parallel states rather than one point forecast.

![Figure 6 — S1–S4 scenario map](figures/fig-06-s1-s4-scenario-map.svg)

### S1 — Competitive Expansion

Supply elasticity rises, alternative stacks mature, portability improves, and scarcity premiums decline.

The S1 evidence strengthened within the August 28, 2026 evidence cutoff: AMD described Helios rackscale solutions as in production, while Meta committed to **up to 6 GW**, Anthropic to **up to 2 GW**, and Microsoft announced Azure deployment.[^rb6] These are deployment / shipment commitments rather than measured utilization or production-workload share, so they strengthen the competitive branch without displacing the current S2 baseline by themselves.

### S2 — Baseline Concentration

High growth and concentration coexist. Leading platforms and scarce-layer suppliers retain strong economics while substitution paths continue to expand.

**This is the current evidence baseline as of August 2026.**

### S3 — Resource Hegemony

Multiple scarce layers, quantity assurance / delivery access, switching costs, and financing coordination reinforce one another while workload monetization remains sufficient to support the associated commitments, increasing the cost of replicating a competitive system.

### S4 — Capital Hard Landing

Utilization, monetization, clearing prices, commitments, or financing quality fail to validate the expanding capital base across multiple actors and layers.

The scenarios are not sequential and do not carry fixed probabilities.

---

## 10. What would change the current view

The current S2 interpretation should not be defended against contrary evidence.

The highest-value reverse signals include:

- durable loosening in HBM and advanced packaging;
- large-scale alternative-stack production substitution with low migration cost;
- materially broader quantity assurance / delivery access across multiple qualified scarce layers;
- Time-to-Power shortening enough to stop differentiating high-value projects;
- major forward commitments being cancelled, rescheduled, or materially reduced;
- sustained deterioration in utilization, AI revenue, clearing prices, and customer cash generation;
- supplier-assisted financing increasing while independent financing and utilization weaken;
- new first-party evidence materially changing China's Production-Grade Gates or autonomous frontier closure;
- regulatory remedies materially changing interface access, tying, or entry conditions.

The framework is designed so that new evidence can change the conclusion.

---

## 11. Research discipline

The report uses:

> **F → H → M → S → X**

- **F — Fact:** observed and publicly verifiable;
- **H — Hypothesis:** a future input condition;
- **M — Mechanism:** the causal transmission;
- **S — Scenario:** a conditional future state;
- **X — Falsification:** evidence strong enough to force the judgment to change.

Evidence is also separated into:

- **A:** first-party / formal evidence;
- **B:** institutional / academic research;
- **C:** sell-side / supply-chain / media estimate;
- **D:** report-side calculation / sensitivity / scenario input.

The core rule is simple:

> **Future analysis can be strong, but the fact layer, denominator, evidence identity, and time identity must remain conservative.**

---

## Bottom line

The AI infrastructure buildout is best understood as a reordering of industrial priority across a complete delivery system.

The decisive variables are not GPU shipments alone.

They are:

- who can assemble and operate the system stack;
- who can secure the next unit of qualified scarce capacity;
- how quickly HBM, packaging, networking, and power constraints move;
- whether alternative stacks reduce migration cost and concentration;
- whether traditional end systems retain sufficient residual access;
- whether long-duration commitments and financing structures convert into utilization;
- whether installed compute produces verified workflow output and durable cash flow.

The current evidence supports **S2 — Baseline Concentration**; it does not support a conclusion of permanent monopoly, automatic competitive diffusion, or a confirmed capital hard landing.

For the complete evidence, denominators, counterarguments, and falsification boundaries, read the [32-chapter canonical English report](README.md), the [List of Figures](01-list-of-figures.md), and the [Core Evidence Ledger](../核心证据台账.en.md).
